cands.name: Laurel Lee
cands.bio: Republican U.S. Representative since January 2023. Former Florida Secretary of State (2019-2022), Hillsborough circuit judge (2013-2019), federal prosecutor and public defender. University of Florida B.A. and J.D. Married to former Florida Senate President Tom Lee.
cands.local_ties: Lives in the Brandon area of Hillsborough County (Wikipedia). Born at Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio; Air Force family.

record.text: Committees: Energy and Commerce; Judiciary; House Administration (vice chair of the committee and chair of its Elections subcommittee).

Lead sponsor of the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act (FISA Section 702 reauthorization); introduced the bipartisan DEFIANCE Act on non-consensual deepfake images; named an impeachment manager in the 2024 Mayorkas case; House AI task force member.

Introduced a proposed constitutional amendment limiting federal voting to U.S. citizens; her HEAR Act (Holocaust-era art recovery) passed the House in March 2026 (per her official site search listing).

money_notes.text: Endorsed by AIPAC, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, ClearPath Foundation, Maggie's List and the Associated Builders and Contractors Florida Gulf Coast Chapter (per Wikipedia).
Wikipedia reports her reported net worth rose from $7.39 million (2022) to $14.02 million (2024), with about $6.2 million in publicly traded assets as of January 2026 (citing Quiver Quantitative).

endorsements.text: Donald Trump; sheriffs Chad Chronister (Hillsborough), Chris Nocco (Pasco), Al Nienhius (Hernando), David Vincent (Citrus); U.S. Chamber of Commerce; AIPAC; ClearPath; Maggie's List; Associated Builders and Contractors Florida Gulf Coast Chapter (per Wikipedia).

cands.gaps: No controversies listed in Wikipedia or found elsewhere in the sources reviewed. The new District 15 boundaries (Hernando, Citrus, parts of Pasco and Hillsborough) are from news summaries, not an official map I opened. Campaign social handles not verified. Owner-source search surfaced only a 2023 Rumble title I could not tie to her.

votes.what: Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.
Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

cands.name: Robert People
cands.bio: Democratic nominee; retired U.S. Army veteran (journalist/ammunition specialist, 1997-2018) and writer; most recently a senior proposal writer (iQor, 2024-2025). First run for office. Won the Aug. 18 primary 53.6% to 46.4%. Supports Medicare for All and a ban on congressional stock trading.

record.text: U.S. Army service 1997-2018; has not held elected office per his BallotReady profile.

money_notes.text: Endorsed post-primary by Track AIPAC (per Wikipedia). FEC: about $82,500 raised through Oct. 14, 2026, mostly individual contributions plus a $10,440 candidate loan that has been repaid.
